metadata.title: How Your Phone Types Japanese
metadata.narration_policy: Narration is SCRIPT.md verbatim, one script section per beat. Beat IDs B01-B11 match script sections 1-11; BVDT, BHTF and BOUT are sections 12, 13 and 14.
metadata.visual_policy: Simple illustrative graphics only: kana, kanji, candidate lists, probability bars, word-split paths. No real product logos and no screenshots of commercial apps. Any IME candidate list is an illustrative animation, not a screenshot. The Claude composer, verdict page and the channel mark are redrawn bookends, not screenshots.

fonts.rule: Every Manim Text containing kana or kanji sets font='Hiragino Sans' (or a listed fallback) explicitly; never the default font. Verify glyphs in the rendered frame, not the source.

portrait_layout.rule: In 9:16, all text and labels sit above 86% of the frame height (y < 0.86 * H), leaving the bottom 14% empty.

metadata.library_check: Searched with ./art scenes first. Reused: ClaudeComposerAsk, BrutalistHesitantWriter, ClaudeVerdictArtifact, LogoOutro (and their 916 variants). No library match for kana/kanji candidate fans, IME scoring paths or word-split paths, so those beats are custom Manim scenes; the misses are logged by the search in TEMPLATE-MISSES.md.
metadata.reformat: full-length; native portrait graphics; preserve source framing

beats.narration_text: Hi, I am Keya and this video is about how your phone types Japanese, and why every Japanese sentence you type is a guess. The voice you're hearing is an AI voice reading my script.

show.event: the ask types in under 'Hi, Keya'
three result lines land: the keyboard, the guess, the AI voice
the AI-voice disclosure is spoken while the answered composer holds

props.command: Explain how my phone keyboard types Japanese, and why every sentence is a guess.

beats.narration_text: I've been learning Japanese on Duolingo for over a year, and hana still trips me up: flower or nose? Now my keyboard has the same problem. I type hashi. Bridge, chopsticks, or edge? It has to guess.

shot.visual_intent: Two homophone fans: hana splits into flower and nose, then hashi splits into bridge, chopsticks and edge. A drawn keyboard bar then shows one typed sound with three candidates and a question mark.

show.event: 'hana' drawn in kana (はな) with two kanji branches, 花 'flower' and 鼻 'nose', on 'flower or nose?'
a drawn keyboard bar types 'hashi'; はし appears
three candidates fan out: 橋 bridge, 箸 chopsticks, 端 edge
a question mark lands over the three: 'it has to guess'

beats.narration_text: Autocomplete feels like a new AI trick. But Japanese keyboards were predicting words long before chatbots. Let's see how they guess which word you mean.

show.event: the writer types 'Autocomplete is a new AI trick.' in terracotta
it pauses, then deletes the whole sentence
'Japanese keyboards were predicting words long before chatbots.' types in ink
the corrected sentence holds while the voice says 'Let's see how they guess'

props.text:
Autocomplete
is a new
AI trick.

beats.note: Beat 3 per Keya: typed 'Autocomplete is a new AI trick.' then corrected to 'Japanese keyboards were predicting words long before chatbots.' The whole sentence is the trigger phrase so the correction replaces the sentence, not one word. Verify after render: beat media >= 8 s and the corrected sentence is fully on screen before the cut; portrait uses BrutalistHesitantWriter916. The corrected sentence is typed over two lines (a line break replaces the space after 'predicting') so it fits inside the title-safe margin at this size. 9:16 only: bigger type over more lines (line breaks stand in for spaces) so the smallest text clears the portrait type floor.

qc.sparse_reason: Hesitant-writer overview (BrutalistHesitantWriter): the sentence is typed token by token, so a mid-beat frame is mostly cream by design. Only the underfill and clustered checks are waived; edge-bleed, empty-frame and contrast still apply. The corrected sentence is split over two lines so it stays inside the title-safe margin.

beats.narration_text: Japanese is spoken by more than a hundred and twenty million people, mostly in Japan. And it's written without spaces between words.

shot.visual_intent: A counter climbs to 'more than 120 million speakers' beside a drawn map-free dot field; then a sentence in Japanese runs together with no gaps and slash marks try to find word edges.

show.event: a speaker counter rises to '120 million+' and a caption 'mostly in Japan' lands (no map, no flag)
a line of Japanese text (日本語を話す人は多い) is drawn as an unbroken run of glyphs
an empty gap marker pulses where an English space would be: 'no spaces between words'

beats.narration_text: Japanese has three ways of writing, often mixed in a single sentence. Hiragana carries the grammar. Katakana is for foreign words, like my own name, Keya. And kanji carry meaning: two different kanji can share one sound, like flower and nose, both read hana.

shot.visual_intent: Three labelled panels land in narration order: hiragana, katakana, kanji; one mixed sentence is colour-coded by script; then two kanji share the sound hana.

show.event: a mixed Japanese sentence draws in with each script tinted: hiragana ink, katakana terracotta, kanji underlined
'Hiragana: the grammar' lands on the hiragana strokes
'Katakana: foreign words' lands; Keya's name is drawn in katakana (ケヤ)
'Kanji: meaning' lands; 花 and 鼻 slide in side by side
both resolve to 'hana' underneath

beats.narration_text: On a keyboard, I type Latin letters. H-A-S-H-I becomes はし in hiragana. A simple kana keyboard stops right there. But はし could be three different words, so a real Japanese keyboard, called an IME, has one more job: choosing the kanji.

shot.visual_intent: A drawn keyboard bar types H-A-S-H-I key by key; the letters turn into はし; a kana-only keyboard stops there with a stop mark; an IME box then opens with the extra job.

show.event: five keys light in order: H, A, S, H, I
the letters fold into はし
a stop line: 'a simple kana keyboard stops here'
three question marks appear over はし: 'three different words'
an 'IME' box opens with the label 'choosing the kanji'

beats.narration_text: Japanese has many words like that. Hashi is bridge, chopsticks or edge. Hana is flower or nose. Ame is rain or candy. Shiro is white or castle. Same sounds, different kanji.

shot.visual_intent: Four homophone pairs or triples build as a drawn table, one row per spoken word, each row splitting one kana sound into its kanji.

show.event: row 1: はし splits into 橋 bridge, 箸 chopsticks, 端 edge on 'hashi'
row 2: はな splits into 花 flower, 鼻 nose on 'hana'
row 3: あめ splits into 雨 rain, 飴 candy on 'ame'
row 4: しろ splits into 白 white, 城 castle on 'shiro'

beats.narration_text: So how does it choose? The IME lists every way to split my kana into words, and every kanji for each piece. It scores each option by how common the word is, and how often those words appear together in real Japanese text. Then it picks the highest-scoring path.

shot.visual_intent: The IME performs itself on one kana string, はしをわたる: tick marks show every way to split it, each piece sprouts its kanji (橋を渡る, 箸を渡る, 端を渡る), two illustrative score bars grow on each path (how common the word is; how often the words appear together), and the highest-scoring path is boxed while the others fade to 40%. The paths are illustrative and the bars carry no numbers.

show.event: はしをわたる appears at the top
two tick marks show where it can be split: 'every way to split'
each piece sprouts its kanji: three paths, 橋を渡る, 箸を渡る, 端を渡る
bars grow on 'how common the word is'
a second bar grows on 'how often those words appear together'; 'illustrative bars, not real numbers' appears
the longest path (橋を渡る) is boxed; the others fade to 40%

beats.narration_text: Without spaces, even splitting is a guess. This sentence can mean "take off your shoes here" or "take off your kimono here." A person uses the situation: at the front door, it's shoes. The IME only has statistics: which split appears more often in text.

shot.visual_intent: ここではきものをぬぐ large in kana with romaji underneath, split two ways one above the other with は highlighted where it moves, each resolving to kanji, an English gloss and a simple outline (shoe, kimono); then side by side, 'You: where you are' (front-door outline pointing to footwear) and 'IME: which split is more common in text' (two illustrative bars, footwear longer, no numbers).

show.event: ここではきものをぬぐ appears large in kana with kokodehakimonowonugu underneath
it splits two ways, one above the other, with は highlighted: ここで / はきもの / を / ぬぐ and ここでは / きもの / を / ぬぐ
top path resolves: ここで履物を脱ぐ, 'Take off your footwear here', shoe outline
bottom path resolves: ここでは着物を脱ぐ, 'Take off your kimono here', kimono outline
side by side: 'You: where you are', a front-door outline pointing to the footwear
'IME: which split is more common in text', two bars, footwear longer, labelled 'illustrative'

manim.font_note: Japanese in Hiragino Sans; 9:16 native layout in vertical/scenes.py, stacked, text above 86% of the height.

beats.narration_text: This isn't new. In 1978, Toshiba unveiled the first Japanese word processor. It converted kana to kanji with a dictionary and grammar rules, and chose between homophones using sentence context and how often words are used. Later keyboards counted words in huge amounts of text. Today, neural networks called Transformers, the same design behind ChatGPT, are helping keyboards convert as you type.

shot.visual_intent: A three-stop timeline: a dictionary-and-grammar machine, keyboards that count words in large text, then Transformer networks that convert as you type.

show.event: stop 1: a drawn word-processor outline lands on the spoken year; 'dictionary + grammar rules'; two homophone candidates weighed by 'sentence context' and 'how often used'
stop 2: a pile of text pages feeds a counter: 'counted words in huge amounts of text'
stop 3: letters arrive one at a time and the converted text grows after them: 'neural networks called Transformers help keyboards convert as you type' (no ChatGPT logo)

beats.narration_text: It still makes mistakes. Names and brand-new words may not be in its dictionary, so it can split them in the wrong place or pick the wrong kanji.

shot.visual_intent: A name (けや) and a 'brand-new word' card go into an IME box; a dictionary lookup comes back 'no entry'; then the kana is cut in the wrong place (a tick mark) and the wrong kanji (毛, 矢) are offered and marked.

show.event: けや and a 'brand-new word' card go into the IME box
a dictionary page is searched with a magnifier: 'no entry'
けや is cut in the wrong place (a tick mark): 'cut in the wrong place'
two wrong kanji, 毛 and 矢, are offered and marked with crimson crosses: 'the wrong kanji'

beats.note: Last sentence removed by Keya's decision. See FACTCHECK.md: the remaining claims are supported in outline.

beats.narration_text: Kanji confused me at first, but they're the reason hana can mean flower or nose without confusion. The keyboard just has to guess which one I mean, and so do I, every lesson. Every time your phone suggests a word, it's doing what ChatGPT does: predicting what comes next. Japanese keyboards were doing it decades earlier.

show.event: the artifact page opens on the title
the heading lands: the keyboard guesses, and so do I
the closing line lands on 'predicting what comes next'

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude: Show me how predictive typing works in Japanese, English and Korean. What's the same, and what's hardest in each? Look at how each language splits words, and where guessing gets hard. And next time you type, watch the suggestion bar. It's a tiny language model guessing for you.

show.event: the suggested prompt types into the composer
the prompt holds on screen while the voice discusses it

props.command: Show me how predictive typing works in Japanese, English and Korean. What's the same, and what's hardest in each?
